notes: Counts describe the first-pass text only (111 sentence/item claims; 24 unsupported, 3 textbook). Two supported sentences were added to article section 3 (rows c112, c113, not counted) because cuts left it under 110 words; they also tie the diabetes related links to sources. Doubts: (1) '1 in 7 babies' comes from a Kingston and Richmond NHS Foundation Trust leaflet seen only through a search summary (the search tool also said the underlying study was not found); it is now attributed to that trust and the leaflet added to references. (2) '7 to 14 days' is NHS genital thrush wording; scope now explicit (men and women); the oral mouth-gel 7 to 14 days range was not used. (3) Pregnancy sentence: 'third trimester/body changes' not returned and was replaced by CDC and NHS wording; NHS says tablets are not advised, but NHS medicines pages say fluconazole may sometimes be prescribed in pregnancy if other treatments have not worked (not added). (4) Oral thrush and swallowing: NHS lists painful or difficult swallowing as a non-urgent GP reason, but a Welsh NHS patient leaflet advises A&E/999; the page keeps the NHS wording and names GP route only, so a reviewer may want to add a stronger red flag. (5) Related diabetes links kept (type-1 and type-2): sources (NHS, Diabetes UK, MedlinePlus) link thrush to diabetes/high blood sugar but do not distinguish the types.
